title: Explain the Load Balancer and the Rate Limiter — what each does, their algorithms, and the tools used.
shortTitle: Explain the Load Balancer and the Rate Limiter

s1_definition.profdef: A load balancer and a rate limiter are two complementary traffic-management components. A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple backend instances so no single instance is overwhelmed, improving throughput and availability; its algorithms include round-robin, least-connections, weighted, IP-hash, and consistent hashing. A rate limiter restricts how many requests a client may make in a time window, protecting the system from overload and abuse; its algorithms include fixed-window counter, sliding-window log and counter, token bucket, and leaky bucket. The load balancer answers "which instance should handle this request?" while the rate limiter answers "should this request be allowed at all right now?"
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's branch at rush hour. The load balancer is the receptionist who looks at the open counters and sends each customer to whichever one is free, so the work is spread evenly and no clerk drowns while others idle. The rate limiter is the security guard at the door who makes sure no single person tries to submit two hundred forms in one minute, because that would jam the whole branch for everyone else; the guard lets each person through at a fair, sustainable pace and politely asks the rest to wait. One directs traffic to the right place, the other controls how much traffic is allowed in the first place. Together they keep the branch fast and fair even when a crowd arrives.
s1_definition.oneliner: A load balancer spreads requests across instances to answer "where does this go," while a rate limiter caps requests per client over time to answer "should this be allowed right now" — distribution versus protection.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A load balancer and a rate limiter are two complementary traffic-management components. A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple backend instances so no single instance is overwhelmed, improving throughput and availability; its algorithms include round-robin, least-connections, weighted, IP-hash, and consistent hashing. A rate limiter restricts how many requests a client may make in a time window, protecting the system from overload and abuse; its algorithms include fixed-window counter, sliding-window log and counter, token bucket, and leaky bucket. The load balancer answers "which instance should handle this request?" while the rate limiter answers "should this request be allowed at all right now?"

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India's branch at rush hour. The load balancer is the receptionist who looks at the open counters and sends each customer to whichever one is free, so the work is spread evenly and no clerk drowns while others idle. The rate limiter is the security guard at the door who makes sure no single person tries to submit two hundred forms in one minute, because that would jam the whole branch for everyone else; the guard lets each person through at a fair, sustainable pace and politely asks the rest to wait. One directs traffic to the right place, the other controls how much traffic is allowed in the first place. Together they keep the branch fast and fair even when a crowd arrives.

**One line to remember:** A load balancer spreads requests across instances to answer "where does this go," while a rate limiter caps requests per client over time to answer "should this be allowed right now" — distribution versus protection.

sections.s2_technical:
A load balancer sits in front of a pool of identical backend instances and selects one for each request. Its purpose is to spread work evenly so throughput is maximized and no instance saturates while others idle, and it also improves availability by routing only to healthy instances. Load balancers operate at layer four, balancing TCP connections by IP and port, or at layer seven, understanding HTTP so they can route by path, header, or cookie. The common algorithms are round-robin, which rotates through instances in order and is fair for uniform requests; least-connections, which sends each request to the instance with the fewest active requests and handles variable request costs well; weighted variants, which bias toward higher-capacity instances; IP-hash, which maps a client's IP consistently to one instance for session stickiness; and consistent hashing, which routes by a key and remaps only a small fraction of keys when instances change, which suits distributed caches. For example, a layer-seven balancer routes `/api/v1/transfers` to the transfer pool using least-connections while sending `/static/*` to a CDN origin.

A rate limiter restricts how many requests a client may make within a time window, and it exists for a different reason: protection. Without it, a buggy client, a scraper, or a denial-of-service attack can flood the system and degrade service for everyone, so the rate limiter sheds excess load and enforces fair usage, often per API key or per user. When a client exceeds its limit, the server responds with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, usually with a Retry-After hint. The algorithms differ in how they shape traffic. The fixed-window counter counts requests per fixed clock window and is simple but allows a burst of up to twice the limit at the window boundary, because a client can send a full window's worth at the end of one window and again at the start of the next. The sliding-window log keeps timestamps of recent requests and counts those within the trailing window, which is accurate but memory-heavy, while the sliding-window counter approximates this cheaply by blending the current and previous window counts, smoothing the boundary burst. The token bucket refills tokens at a steady rate up to a bucket capacity and lets each request consume a token, which permits controlled bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a long-run average rate. The leaky bucket processes requests at a constant outflow rate regardless of how bursty the input is, smoothing traffic into a steady stream. For example, a token bucket that refills ten tokens per second with a capacity of twenty lets a client burst twenty requests instantly but then settle to ten per second.

The crucial distinction is that these two components solve different problems and are used together, not interchangeably. The load balancer decides placement among healthy instances; the rate limiter decides admission based on client quota. In a typical request path the rate limiter usually runs at the edge or gateway, rejecting excess requests before they consume backend capacity, and the load balancer distributes the admitted requests across instances. The tools reflect this layering. For load balancing, common choices are hardware or cloud layer-four balancers like AWS Network Load Balancer and Azure Load Balancer, layer-seven balancers like Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, AWS Application Load Balancer, and Azure Application Gateway, API gateways like Kong and Spring Cloud Gateway, and in Kubernetes the Service plus kube-proxy with a service mesh like Istio for richer policies. For rate limiting, common choices are gateway features in Kong, Nginx, Spring Cloud Gateway, and API Gateway products, libraries like Bucket4j and Resilience4j RateLimiter in the application, and a shared store like Redis to coordinate limits across many instances. The senior-level point is that a distributed rate limiter must share its counters, typically in Redis, so that the limit is enforced across the whole fleet rather than per instance, otherwise N instances would each allow the full limit and the effective limit would be N times too high.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India exposes a transfer API behind a gateway, with several backend instances.

Problem 1 — during peak hours one backend instance was overwhelmed while others sat idle, because requests were not being spread. This is exactly the load balancer's job: pick a healthy instance per request using an algorithm like least-connections so the load is even.

Problem 2 — a buggy mobile client entered a retry loop and fired thousands of transfer requests per minute from one account, consuming capacity meant for real customers and nearly causing an outage. This is exactly the rate limiter's job: cap requests per client per window and return 429 to the abusive client while everyone else is unaffected.

Problem 3 — a naive first attempt put the rate limiter inside each instance with a local counter, but because there were five instances, each allowed the full per-minute limit, so the effective limit was five times too high and the abuse still got through. This is exactly why a distributed rate limiter must share its counter in Redis so the limit is enforced across the whole fleet.

The mini-project builds a `LoadBalancer` using least-connections to distribute requests, a `TokenBucketRateLimiter` and a `FixedWindowRateLimiter` to show two algorithms, and a `GatewayPipeline` that first rate-limits then load-balances, mimicking the real edge path. The demo sends a normal client and an abusive client through the pipeline, shows the abusive client getting 429 while the normal client is admitted and evenly distributed, and shows the token bucket allowing a controlled burst.

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the gateway (load balancer + rate limiter) demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.gateway.GatewayDemo

# In production, Spring Cloud Gateway does both:
#   lb://transfer-service      → load balancing
#   RequestRateLimiter filter  → Redis-backed token bucket per user
curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers   # watch for HTTP 429 under load

# Nginx alternative (L7 LB + rate limit):
#   upstream transfer { least_conn; server txn-1; server txn-2; server txn-3; }
#   limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m rate=10r/s;
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transfer instances, a token-bucket rate limiter refilling ten tokens per second with a burst capacity of twenty, a normal client making six requests, and an abusive client firing fifty rapid requests.

Step 1: The normal client's first request enters the gateway pipeline. The rate limiter checks the client's token bucket, which starts full, consumes one token, and allows the request. Admission succeeds.

Step 2: The admitted request goes to the load balancer, which picks the instance with the fewest active connections. Because the instances start equal, the first goes to txn-1, and as each subsequent request arrives the balancer picks whichever is least loaded, spreading the six requests across txn-1, txn-2, and txn-3.

Step 3: The normal client's six requests all stay within the bucket, so all six are admitted and the distribution shows them spread across the three instances. The normal customer experiences fast, balanced service.

Step 4: The abusive client fires fifty requests in a tight loop. Its token bucket also starts at capacity twenty, so the first twenty requests each find a token and are admitted as a controlled burst.

Step 5: After twenty requests the bucket is empty, and because the client is firing far faster than the ten-per-second refill, there are no tokens left. Every further request fails the rate-limiter check and receives a 429 Too Many Requests response. Roughly thirty of the fifty are blocked.

Step 6: The gateway totals show the normal client fully served and the abusive client capped, so real customers kept getting fast balanced service while the buggy client was shed at the edge before it could consume backend capacity. This is the two components working together: the rate limiter controlled admission, and the load balancer spread the admitted traffic.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    === Normal client (within limit) ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    normal client spread across instances: {txn-1=2, txn-2=2, txn-3=2}
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  === Abusive client (buggy retry loop) ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 WARNING 429 Too Many Requests for client buggy-client-X (token-bucket)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    abusive client: admitted=20 (burst up to 20), blocked(429)=30
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Gateway totals: accepted=26, rejected=30 (real customers protected)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A load balancer and a rate limiter are two complementary traffic-management components that solve different problems, and the cleanest way to frame them is that the load balancer answers where should this request go, while the rate limiter answers should this request be allowed at all right now. The load balancer sits in front of a pool of identical backend instances and picks one for each request so that work is spread evenly, throughput is maximized, and no single instance saturates while others idle, and it only routes to healthy instances so it also improves availability. Its algorithms are round-robin for uniform requests, least-connections for variable request costs which is usually the best default, weighted variants for a mixed-capacity fleet, IP-hash for session stickiness, and consistent hashing for distributed caches where you want only a small fraction of keys to remap when instances change.

The rate limiter exists for a different reason, which is protection. Without it, a buggy client, a scraper, or a denial-of-service attack can flood the system and degrade service for everyone, so the rate limiter caps how many requests a client may make in a time window, usually per user or per API key, and returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests when the limit is exceeded. Its algorithms shape traffic differently: the fixed-window counter is simple but allows up to a double burst at the window boundary, the sliding-window log is accurate but memory-heavy while the sliding-window counter approximates it cheaply and smooths that boundary burst, the token bucket refills at a steady rate and allows controlled bursts up to the bucket size, and the leaky bucket enforces a constant outflow rate that smooths bursty input into a steady stream.

The key insight I always stress is that they are used together, not instead of each other. In the request path the rate limiter runs at the edge or gateway and sheds excess before it ever reaches the backends, and the load balancer distributes the admitted requests across instances. We hit both needs on our transfer API: during peak hours one instance was overwhelmed while others idled, which the load balancer fixed by spreading load with least-connections, and separately a buggy mobile client in a retry loop fired thousands of requests a minute, which the rate limiter fixed by capping that client and returning 429 while real customers were untouched.

One distributed-systems subtlety I always mention is that a rate limiter across many instances must share its counters, typically in Redis, because if each of five instances keeps a local counter, each allows the full limit and the effective limit is five times too high. We actually made that mistake first with per-instance counters, and the abuse still got through until we moved the counter to Redis so the limit was enforced across the whole fleet. On tools, for load balancing I reach for Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, cloud balancers like AWS Application Load Balancer or Azure Application Gateway, or in Kubernetes a Service with kube-proxy and a service mesh for richer algorithms, and for rate limiting I use gateway features in Kong or Spring Cloud Gateway, libraries like Bucket4j or Resilience4j RateLimiter, backed by Redis for distributed coordination.

The way I summarize it for an interviewer is that the load balancer is about distribution across healthy instances and the rate limiter is about protection through admission control, you put the rate limiter at the edge and the load balancer behind it, and in a distributed deployment you share the rate-limiter state in Redis so the limit holds across the whole fleet.

Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits

Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
